paragraphs.source_en: The representation of mouflon in rock art can also be an indicator of different cultural spheres. Whereas in the Round Head complex there are around three hundred representations of mouflon and antelope, in the Bubaline engravings these animals are almost nonexistent. These engravings are dominated by large wild fauna, mainly water-dependant animals such as elephant or buffalo, which are very rare in the Round Head art. These two styles are thus separated not only geographically but also thematically. Certainly, the animals depicted may reflect their habitat in the period of representation; mouflon and antelope being characteristic for the mountains, other animals being found in the lowlands and lower mountains. However, it would not prevent the prehistoric artists from representing other animal species as well.

paragraphs.source_en: As Aumassip (1986) notices for the lithic industry, different cultures occupy different territories. The notion of territory may also be indicated in the geographical distribution of the rock art, different motifs being particular for different cultures in the Central Sahara.

paragraphs.source_en: Even though we have no proof that the archaeological record can be directly related to the Round Head paintings, several indicators suggest that the Epipalaeolithic and the Mesolithic periods respectively were the crucial phases for this art. The climatic and environmental changes in the Epipalaeolithic period created new opportunities for hunter-gatherers which may have provoked a new way of thinking, possibly stimulating the birth of the new artistic tradition. The new ideology would be represented not only in the paintings, but also in another form of artistic production, the pottery. This important innovative technique is traditionally only considered from the practical point of view but its potential is much greater. The chronological assessment of pottery with the Round Head paintings is examined in the next section.
